“Do you have a moment before you punch out?” she shouted, jogging between the idling van and a support column. “I require an unbiased opinion on a one-take audition reel, and I’ve heard you understand editing cuts better than you speak English.”

Jareth’s hands were clenched tight on the key fob, his hoodie partially zipped, the exhaust heat warming his shins. “If it’s a locked take, you’re finished, correct? A single take implies there are no cuts left to discover.”

“The performance runs three minutes and five seconds; the judges demand exactly three minutes. I need to vanish for four heartbeats somewhere in that sequence.”

He scratched at an invisible itch beneath his cuff. “Four beats is simple—mute the background track for two counts, and the error fades into the floor.”

“That is cheating. They will detect the gap in the drums. I need the dance to be seamless, not the audio.”

“Then slice your landing after the barrel turn; audiences blink during moments of shock anyway.”

Nerea stepped between the bollards, her sock saturated by gutter water. “The landing is live sound—the foot strikes concrete. You can’t lower that volume. Try again.”

“Look, I’m about to go off the clock; go to the editing lab tomorrow, someone there owes you favors twelve deep.”

She adjusted the speaker in her pocket; 7/8 cymbals hissed like restless cats. “The lab is booked until Thursday. You have the software on that ancient laptop in your van.”

His shoulders rose in a slow-motion shrug. “The software is outdated and the screen is damaged enough that you need tweezers to count the pixels. Take it to a real professional, yes?”

“Five minutes, in your van. I will bring an external drive and snacks; you drive, I trim during red lights.”

“Red lights here last twenty seconds at most—hardly enough time to connect the drive. You will just give yourself motion sickness.”

She nudged her dropped sneaker with a bare toe, her jaw set. “Then cut it for me now. Phone edit, free favor, I owe you one back-row ticket forever.”

The van door creaked open, exhaling a cloud of stale fry smell. “Make the deadline tomorrow, not tonight. Don't upload a messy cut; upload raw and call it ‘artistic restraint.’ Judges love the taste of ego.”

Nerea watched him retreat inside, the door slam echoing down the empty deck like a snare drum hit cut too short. Her thumb hovered over the cracked screen, showing 3:05 in red. Somewhere within that file lived the missing four beats, concealed behind sweat and concrete. She pulled her sock on, turned off the speaker, and began to walk. Editing labs reopen on Thursday; the upload was due Friday. If she couldn’t delete the seconds, she might still outrun them.

The senior center retained its customary December aroma: a mix of radioactive cinnamon and instant coffee that stained the tongue the color of bargain-bin carpet. Folding tables bowed beneath the weight of everyone’s nostalgic crafts: star-shaped cookie cutters, dented pie tins, and the obligatory pipe-cleaner candy canes. Gul hunched over a six-inch square of roofing tin scavenged from a storm, sleeves rolled up high, black fingerprints marking where the metal had fought back. Across the table, decorated with vinyl snowflakes, Hristo held a leaking reindeer mug as if it contained state secrets. His arm hair had turned silver, and his forearms were laddered with pale scars—each one a quiet résumé of forty years persuading sheet metal to behave.

Gul skipped small talk. “I want it to reflect light like a mirror, but every time I fold the edges, they remain sharp enough to draw blood. How do I fix that without dulling the surface?”

Hristo didn’t look up. “You’re folding once and leaving it. Do a double fold, a quarter inch in, then flatten the seam with the flat face of the hammer. It cuts the edge and hides the burr.”

Gul’s eyebrow twitched—a single beat of an impatient metronome. “Won’t that ruin the crisp line? I’m aiming for a snowflake—details smaller than an eighth of an inch.”

For the first time, Hristo offered a small smile, like a man discovering he enjoyed the song on the radio. “The crisp line remains if you score first. Use a ball-peen to mark the inside score, then bend on the score with needle-nose pliers. The metal follows the rule rather than your thumbs guessing.” He demonstrated with invisible tools, his wrists loose, muscle memory humming.

Gul tilted the tin, checking angles that would concern only calculus majors. “What about reflection? The folded edge blocks half the angle.”

“The fold is on the back. The front face stays flat.” Hristo tapped the table twice for emphasis. “Use 320-grit sponge after folding, light circles, six passes—it removes the micro-burr and polishes.”

Gul’s voice pared down to the bare essentials. “Any trick for the back without hiding the hammer texture?”

“Skip the sponge on texture zones.” Hristo reached for a roll of blue painter’s tape, tearing a sliver with absent-minded precision. “Mask with painter’s tape cut to the silhouette, polish around it, then peel after.”

He returned the roll, its end fluttering like surrender. Gul’s fingers drummed. “How long does the sponge last before it clogs?”

“These tins shred cheap sponges in ten ornaments.” He shrugged, the kind of shrug that had once reset radial-arm saws. “Rinse under hot tap, rub with your thumb, let it dry in two minutes, and it’s good as new.”

Gul nodded once, economical. “Easy enough. Thanks—I figured I’d have to grind.”

Hristo lifted the reindeer mug in a motion too smooth to be a toast and too definite to be a dismissal. “Grinding eats tin thickness faster than rust. Keep the hammer singing, and the tin behaves.”

Somewhere up front, the glue guns coughed to life. Neither moved toward them yet; the tin in Gul’s hand, under the tired December light, was finally behaving.

Aminata’s mouse wheel shuddered under her thumb, producing the weary click she had come to despise. Sixteen council districts, a single stakeholder package, and three hours remaining. She watched Spencer saunter past her desk, his backpack perched high, earbuds dangling like escaped IV lines. On the whiteboard behind him, someone had scrawled “SPENCER = SCRIPT GUY” in permanent marker. She accepted this as a sign.

“Can you show me how to batch-export these maps? I need to generate sixteen PDFs by five.”

Spencer did not slow down. “The scripting wiki is on SharePoint. Check there first; it’s quite comprehensive.”

The overhead fluorescents buzzed, sounding like cheap cicadas. Aminata swiveled her chair to block the aisle. “I looked—I couldn’t find the loop sample for data-driven pages. Just two minutes of your time?”

He tapped his watch face: 3:11. “I am literally leaving. There’s a bus in four minutes. Sorry.”

She grabbed her laptop, the power cord trailing behind like a snake. “Walk with me to the plotter, then. You just need to tell me which toolbox contains the iterator.”

They shuffled forward three desks, Spencer scanning for an escape route. “I always used ModelBuilder, never Python. You’ll need someone who codes.”

“ModelBuilder is fine,” she said, her voice bright with concession. “Can you open your old model so I can copy it?”

Spencer side-stepped the printer tray, coffee dripping onto obsolete floodplain flyers. “It’s on the retired server. IT wiped most of that data after the ransomware incident.”

Aminata nodded toward the whiteboard. “Really? You’re the only one listed on the whiteboard for automation.”

“The whiteboard is outdated. You should bug IT—policy says they keep backups.”

She felt her carpal tunnel drumming a tiny rhythm against her tendons. “IT ticket turnaround is two days. I need these maps tonight.”

Spencer reached the coatrack, his fingers drumming against the rubber-band ball he kept there. Snap, snap. Countdown. “Then manually export. Fluorescent duct tape, right click, repeat. It gets the job done.”

“That’s forty-eight clicks every run. My wrist is already buzzing.”

He slung on his bag, the bus ticket fluttering like a surrender flag. “Occupational hazard. Look, I absolutely don’t have time to stay. Good luck.”

The door clicked shut behind him; Aminata stared at the bagel labeled “Monday,” now a historical artifact. The plotter exhaled warm mechanical breath onto her ankles. She reopened the SharePoint page, her fingers hovering. Forty-eight clicks, sixteen times. The overhead lights kept score.

The overhead fluorescents hummed with the irritating drone of cheap insects as Selah stood ankle-deep in sawdust, her backpack straps pulling her shoulders down toward the floor. She had walked directly from the library, three heavy books on colonial smuggling still digging into her spine, and now stood before a stack of lumber that seemed taller than her future income.

"Can I ask you about wood that won't cause a sliding lid to jam?" she asked the clerk who was restocking off-cuts.

The clerk straightened up, his navy cap a dull, dishwater color. "I’m happy to help. What size box?"

"About six by eight inches, with walls half an inch thick."

His pencil scratched across a black notebook already covered in a spiderweb of numbers. "Go with quartersawn cherry. It’s stable, cuts cleanly, and doesn’t cost a fortune."

She squinted at the prices scrawled in chalk. "Will it warp?"

"Almost not at all if you seal the end grain. It’s for indoor use, correct?"

"Yes, a bedroom shelf." Selah tapped a maple board. "Wouldn’t mahogany look richer?"

"Sapele is its cheaper cousin. It looks posh, but it moves in the summer. Stick with cherry."

She continued to touch the boards, her fingers nervous. There were twenty days until graduation, and nineteen until the family brunch where her gift would be missing.

"I have 240-grit sandpaper at home—is that good enough?"

"Perfect. Cherry burnishes well at 240 grit; you don’t need to chase a glass-smooth finish."

The caliper caught her eye, its red handle bright against the gloom of aisle twelve. She grabbed it, squeezing the jaws open and shut, open and shut, like a mechanical crab. "Is there any trick for the groove so the lid doesn’t stick?"

The guy paused, his hand resting on a short walnut off-cut destined for no one’s project. "Cut it a hair wide, then wax the tongue. Expansion leaves breathing room."

"Hair meaning...?"

He slid a business card between two stacked off-cuts. "Slip a playing card through; if it drags, hit it once more with the plane."

The card slid smoothly. He gave a satisfied nod that Victor would have made if he’d just cracked a crossword clue in ink.

"And what’s the glue-up order?"

"Ends first, long grain last. Clamps every four inches; cherry forgives if you rush."

She exhaled. She hung the caliper back on its hook. "Price check—will twenty bucks cover it?"

"Easily. Cherry is $6.40 a foot; you need half a foot. Grab a scrap from the cart to save more."

She found a board about eight inches long, scarred but workable, keeping half her pizza budget intact. Tonight, she would drag the kitchen table to the center, open the windows for sawdust snow, and keep sanding until something slid open without sticking.

Behind her, Victor returned to his notebook, already totaling board-feet for strangers who might never know what good advice cost.

Slanted afternoon sun bars the cutting board and the IT8 target taped to it, resembling a stark ransom demand. Oksana’s finger taps a rhythm on the counter; a single grain of Cyan remains stuck to her knuckle, a relic from the morning’s committee gathering and the lingering critique of being “visually noisy.” She scrutinizes the proof held in the viewing booth, where the greens appear to sag into a sickly mustard hue. “The greens must match the original lithograph, not this swamp water.” Her tone is sharp and brief, offering no room for pleasantries.

Theocharis is midway through stuffing his backpack when her words reach him. He pauses, contemplating the silent print head, then sets the bag down. Being helpful is the easiest stance to adopt when the issue is color rather than connectivity. “Berwald is attempting to render green using only four inks. Begin with an IT8 scan and a new profile.”

Oksana brushes her hair aside, her face already wearing a *I-told-you-so* expression. “I already did that. It’s still muddy.” A slight twitch of impatience moves her tapping foot.

“What illuminant setting did you use?” he asks, pulling the spectrophotometer closer. The machine hums with the lethargic vibration of a cat that refuses to purr.

“I kept it at D50. Should I switch to D65?”

He tilts the i1, inspecting its silver nozzle. “D65 is warmer; you’ll struggle with it for weeks. Instead, cap the black point, around L 12, and pull the midpoint back by three.”

“That will clip my shadows,” she says, her jaw tightening.

Theocharis unclips the power cord, looping it through his fingers like a jump rope. “Clipping is preferable to neon. The profile must also align with the paper’s profile; which RIP are you using?”

“ImagePrint.”

“Excellent. Turn off ‘absolute colorimetric’; it makes the spectrophotometer less compliant with white point adjustments.”

Oksana’s cursor activates on the adjacent screen; the mouse click sounds like a period. “Done. Where should I anchor the neutral foil? It’s casting blue.”

“Use a new reference file. Grab the 30% gray patch, subtract 3 from ‘b’, and re-export the .ti1.”

She types without glancing at the keys. “Three clicks south in ‘b’, re-export complete.” Sweat beads at her temple—the temperature control lamp baking the sealed room like a greenhouse.

He checks the i1 with an expert touch. “Remake the measurement, but let the i1 cool first—it gets erratic when hot.”

“How long to wait?” She looks at the wall clock, as if seconds might have already escaped.

Theocharis raises the metal can of compressed air and releases a short white jet that dissipates into vapor. “Two minutes. You can squeeze the cup; absolutely don’t brew it like espresso.”

She actually smiles, a first sign of tension breaking. “I have two minutes. After the profile—should I do a test print first?”

“Yes, a single 8×10 strip focused only on the green range. Compare it under south light first, then in the booth.” He points to the dusty louvers, those slats where sunlight still seems to kneel.

Oksana rolls her shoulders as if releasing tension from cables. The committee meeting feels distant now. “What about the certification form?”

Theocharis shrugs off his pack again, prepared for this final step. “Check ‘custom perceptual’ on the last line, add the date, and you’re set.” He offers the chair; she slides into its residual warmth.

Jasmina shoved a plastic chair toward Levent with the heel of her boot, the screech echoing across the canvas floor. “I’m swamped in second-by-second skin temperature data—how do I boil that down to a single red flag for each firefighter?”

Levent balanced his laptop on one knee, the cooler beneath him shifting like an unwilling seat. “Apply a rolling maximum over ninety-second windows, then flag anything two standard deviations above each person’s pre-drill baseline. It gives you a simple go/no-go.”

She tapped the trackpad, watching rows of data scroll faster than her heartbeat. “Fine, but two sigma catches half the crew in an Alabama summer. I need higher specificity.”

He grinned, glad his theory held up in practice. “Simple—raise the threshold to three sigma AND require the trend to last three minutes; that caps false positives unless the sun is actively trying to kill them.”

“Right, the fog of post-exercise suppression skews the baseline—how do I separate that?”

Levent tapped the lid of her laptop. “Discard the first five minutes after exit, wait for the heart rate to drop below one-ten; whatever registers after that is genuine heat load, not an anxiety spike.”

She scribbled a note, the letters sharp and brief. “That makes sense, but trainees chug water immediately—skin temp plummets then rebounds—how do I cut out that artifact?”

“Label it as a ‘cooling period,’ exclude it from the slope calculation; use hydration timestamps as masks, expect mean reversion within two minutes, ignore it.”

Jasmina looked at a table where half-filled cups formed a jagged skyline. “I only logged water at the buckets, not individual sips; there are some data gaps here.”

“Interpolate between known hydration events—linear is fine, this isn’t an ICU study—then label questionable windows with a low-confidence flag, review them manually later.”

The word *manually* stung beneath her ribs. “Manual means me at two a.m.—I need a filter to auto-exclude obvious sensor drops, too.”

“Simple dropouts are any reading that jumps ten degrees in one second—censor the adjacent five-second buffer, use a majority vote across the three nearest sensors to patch.”

She exhaled, feeling a small win. “Great. Once I have clean flags, should I average them or take the worst episode per shift?”

He leaned back, palms resting on his thighs. “For the policy uplink: the worst single sustained episode per individual. Regulations love absolute peaks, not convoluted averages.”

“Just output that timestamp, value, and individual ID—CSV line? JSON?”

“CSV, three columns. Chiefs open it in Excel like sacred scripture. Deliver it nightly via sftp to the ‘Rehab Dashboard’ folder—it’s already whitelisted.”

“I can script that tonight; thanks, Levent. I owe you cold pizza.”

He snapped the lid shut, steam fogging his glasses. “Make it half-vegetarian and we’re even; bring the chips, too.”

She chuckled, the sound surprising them both over the hiss of the leaking hose, and clicked the band on her clipboard.

The air in the back office reeked of old fryer grease and the adhesive meant to hold the carpet flat. Despite this, Bastian’s shirt stuck to his back; he had run down the corridor again seeking any solution, but only Nirmala remained, her face partially illuminated by relentless produce notifications. She perched on her rolling chair as if ready to flee, her thumb hovering over her phone.

“Hi Nirmala—got two minutes? I’m trying to map out a soft launch for the digital menu.”

She glanced up, polite but already distracted. “I’m sorry, I’m just the produce person. Systems is three doors down; ask Colin.”

“Colin is on vacation until Thursday. I’m stuck on phased deployments. Can you tell me if there’s a standard sequence for trail stores?”

A green alert pinged across her glasses. She sighed. “Everyone I know uses random argon flow or coin flips—it’s not predictable.”

“Sure, but there must be a risk matrix. Older POS systems first, then high-volume ones?”

“Check with Marketing—I only move tomatoes from A to B.”

Bastian’s cheek twitched. “You helped track the beta tables last spring. That’s rollout data, isn’t it?”

“That was an emergency inventory salvage, totally different animal.”

“Still, do you recall if the Riverfront branch crashed during peak lunch? That’s useful intel.”

The edge of her tote squeaked against the chair. “All I remember is we ran out of jalapeños by Tuesday.”

He took a breath, keeping his tone reasonable. “Look, if I show up Monday with no prep, they’ll assign me mop duty. Could you forward me the old incident tickets?”

“I don’t have ticket access; I’m literally capped at spreadsheets full of apples.”

“Then point me—who actually owns menu deployment? I’ve been tossed around like cold fries.”

She shrugged. “Honestly? Venue tech, but half are contractors and the other half are at a conference in Vegas. Hashtag sorry.”

Bastian leaned back; the HDMI cable under his heel hissed across the tile. “So I’m supposed to stall until a taxi brings Colin from McCarran? That’s a disaster plan.”

“Or just pilot one store, gather bullet points, and hope nobody yells.”

“One store limits the data set; my prof wants full cohort variance.”

“Then take the downtown express bus to Systems and plant yourself outside the server cage.”

“They’ll see an intern with a lanyard and infrared badge and boot me in three seconds.”

She stood up, her chair wheeling away. “Not my circus—I’ve got a produce call in sixty seconds down in the loading bay.”

“One last thing—can I at least screengrab the past three months’ sales by hour from your dashboard? That’s neutral territory.”

With her hand already on the door, she delivered her final deflection. “Dashboard auto-wipes at end of cycle; don't try to grab anything. Try Finance?”

Bastian watched the foamcore menus tremble overhead, heard the hallway echo of jalapeño crates being counted, and wondered if anyone here cared about software half as much as vegetables.

The corner grocery store resembled a generous walk-in closet, illuminated by the hum of strip lights and the scent of wilting cilantro in plastic bags. Low, orange sunlight seeped through the glass. With Ramadan beginning the next day, the narrow aisles pulsed with the rush of last-minute shoppers.

Yannis bumped the automatic door open with his hip, his backpack pressing against his spine. He had twenty dollars, nine meals to cover, and ten minutes before the campus shuttle arrived. He snatched a dented basket and tapped it against his shoe: one, two, three.

Behind the counter, Ibtisam stacked cans of ful like bricks, the brim of her cap casting a shadow over her eyes. The wall clock indicated she had forty-one minutes left—forty-one minutes of saying “Sure, we have that” before her ride could pull away from the curb.

Yannis approached, his basket rattling. “Excuse me—what is the quickest, most filling thing I can cook after the lab?”

“Get a can of ful; heat it, eat it, done.” She didn’t look up, continuing to layer the metal rectangles.

Dollar signs flickered behind his eyes. “I have nine nights to cover with twenty bucks; cans get expensive. Any bulk options?”

A carton thudded into place. “Try the bigger supermarket two blocks down; they sell sacks of lentils.”

“I’m on foot, and the shuttle leaves in eight minutes. Is there something here?”

She nudged the date rack. “Rice and dates are on sale. They’re filling, cheap, and shelf-stable.”

Plain rice at midnight sounded like wet gravel. “Plain rice? It takes forty minutes to cook after I get home; I’ll be eating at midnight.”

“Soak it while you work and finish it later. Or buy instant if you’re that late.”

He pictured last week’s instant rice: white confetti glued together with tap water. “Instant tastes like confetti. Is there a protein that cooks faster?”

She pried open another carton. “Eggs, aisle three. Ask the cashier; I have boxes to unload.”

“Eggs spoil if I buy them tonight and can’t cook them until after Ramadan starts.”

She balanced the edge of the box on the shelf, one shoulder already turning away. “Then wait and shop tomorrow; the night hours are posted on the door.”

“I won’t finish my lab work before the shop closes. Help me plan now.”

A sigh escaped before she could suppress it. “Buddy, dates plus peanut butter keeps you alive. Take it or leave it.”

Rice scratched inside his skull; he grabbed the nearest box, sticky against his palm. “Fine, dates. Is the two-kilo box cheaper per dirham?”

Ibtisam checked the clock—thirty-two minutes. “The price is on the sticker; the math is on your phone. I need to clock out.”

The basket finally stopped swinging. With a nod that was less gratitude and more a treaty flagging his defeat, Yannis tucked the dates under his arm. The automatic door exhaled him into the orange light and the counting of stomachs.

A thick blanket of steam rolled over the gravel, carrying the scent of damp straw and leftover espresso toward both of them. Sofiane narrowed his eyes against the haze. The compost piles gleamed like dormant dragons, and his coil apparatus waited in their shadow, ready to be installed only if someone provided him with precise, cold-blooded data. Four hours of sleep had weighed behind his eyes like a sandbag, though caffeine kept propping it up.

He noticed the woman near the shipping container doors, a guitar case in one hand, her posture angled toward the parking lot as if she had already calculated her escape velocity. She looked like someone who enjoyed moving heavy objects or had simply stumbled through every error this farm could produce.

Sofiane cut into her path. “Morning. Is it okay if I ask how you arranged the temperature probes when you tested the compost coils?”

“That wasn’t me. You need Li’s notes—the brown notebook in the lab.” She did not slow down. The guitar case swung like a gate eager to shut.

“I checked. I couldn’t find anything on probe spacing relative to pipe depth. I thought you might recall the intervals you used.”

She continued walking, gravel crunching under her boots. “Sorry, it really wasn’t my project. Maybe the campus energy blog has the specs.”

His laugh was mostly exhaled carbon dioxide. “The blog just says ‘thermistors appropriately zoned.’ That doesn’t give actual distances. Five centimeters? Twenty?”

“It probably depends on the pile diameter. I’m catching a ride, so…” She tilted her wrist to check a watch that wasn’t there, but the gesture still communicated lateness.

A urgent heat crawled across his collarbones, mirroring the warmth radiating from the rows. “A quick guess then—if the core hits 60 Celsius and I want the edge gradient, would three sensors across thirty centimeters be enough?”

She shrugged, the guitar case mimicking the motion. “Sounds about right. Check Smits and Kirk, 2018—they detail thermal mapping in compost columns.”

“I have a new problem,” he said. “It’s a paywalled journal and my access expired yesterday. Could you just tell me the probe layout from Figure 4?”

A small snort escaped her nose, half sympathy, half irritation. “I’d misquote it, mate. Library printer’s two bucks, scan copy in fifteen minutes.”

He raised the battered clipboard between them like a peace flag. “I have coils to install today. A rough sketch on the clipboard—that’s all I need.”

She tapped the board. “Clipboard’s blank, wrong clipboard. Ask operations—tool shed’s past the tomatoes.” The steam rolled back, and for a moment he smelled her retreat instead of compost: city shampoo, coffee going cold on a dashboard.

“Listen,” Sofiane said, softer now but still sharp. “You’ve answered compost questions before, right? Hand to heart, can’t spare forty seconds?”

She stepped backward, already half a stride closer to the asphalt. “Wish I could. Left my coffee cooling. Catch Li tonight—he’s on the five-to-midnight shift.” Then she was gone, the guitar case cutting a wake through the smell of roasting grounds and someone else’s future data.

Sofiane watched the steam close behind her like a curtain. The clipboard dangled, empty. Thirty centimeters. Three probes. Probably.

The breeze from the bay brought the scent of diesel and the metallic clicking of cooling welds into the semi-open garage. Jolene stood by the stripped-out wheel well of the transit bus, her clipboard pressed against her coat like armor that had already failed. She had one page of numbers due the next day; the advisor wanted heat-load calculations, not a narrative. She had tried three online calculators, each producing a different falsehood.

Sameer slid out from beneath the chassis on a creeper, his tools clanking at his hips. A cold drop fell from the chrome trim above and slithered down his collar. He looked up at Jolene’s boots, assessed her shiver, and decided to keep things quick.

“Hey, sorry to bother you—how do you even estimate the heat load for a trailer like this?”

“No problem. The rough rule is: bodies plus losses plus equipment. What is the square footage?”

She recited her notes. “Twenty-eight by eight. There’s a window on the door, a tri-fold exam bench, and one small fridge.”

He wiped his hands on a rag that was already filthy. “Start with the envelope—walls, roof, floor. R-13 is standard here, so the U-value is about point-oh-seven-seven per square foot.”

Her pen paused. “I’m already lost. Can you put it in BTUs?”

“Sure. The interior surface area is around eight-twenty square feet; we use a delta-T of thirty degrees—forty-five outside, seventy-five inside. 820 times .077 times 30 equals one-nine-hundred BTU.”

“That’s just the shell?”

“Just thermal conduction. Then add infiltration—a cheap door gasket means about one air change per hour, adding roughly another eight hundred BTU.”

She scribbled notes. “So we’re at twenty-seven hundred.”

“Plus. The fridge draws two-fifty watts while running, which is another eight-fifty BTU.”

“Thirty-five fifty—does lighting count?”

“Six T8 LED tubes at thirty-five watts each; add two-hundred more, it barely matters.”

Sameer moved a jack-stand aside; the clang echoed. Jolene shifted her weight from one frozen foot to the other. “People are the variable, right?”

“Yes. Two staff and one patient at five-hundred BTU sensible load each: fifteen hundred BTU, spiking to twenty-two fifty if the patient is stressed.”

“And solar load, the sun hitting it?”

Sameer squinted at the unpainted aluminum roof, already glaring under the low sun. “Solar depends on which wall faces south, the color, and shade. An unpainted aluminum roof like this gets nuked. We call it three-hundred BTU per square foot of roof peak at noon—roof area two-twenty—sixty-six hundred BTU baked in.”

“Crud. That pushes us past ten thousand BTU installed.”

He offered a half-smile; his mental calculator had already rounded up. “The smallest mini-split that meets FDA clean-room specs is twelve thousand. It gives you a buffer for a heatwave and a full waiting line.”

“So a fifteen percent fudge factor is sane?”

“Fifteen is generous. Grab the twelve K unit and don't worry about it.”

The clipboard finally stopped shaking. Jolene tore off the top sheet, folded the numbers into her pocket like contraband, and headed for the warm glow of the office, the diesel wind pushing at her back. Behind her, Sameer ducked back under the ribs of the bus again, his tools clinking comfort against the ticking welds.
